ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In chess, a knight can move by jumping to any square whose center is $\sqrt{5}$ units away from the center of the square that it is currently on. For example, a knight on the square marked by the horse in the diagram below can move to any of the squares marked with an “X” and to no other squares. How many ways can a knight on the square marked by the horse in the diagram move to the square with a circle in exactly four moves?

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as an 8 by 8 board. Number rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right; the horse is on square (5,5) and the circle is on square (3,3). From the text, use the knight rule: each move changes coordinates by one of (±1,±2) or (±2,±1), staying on the board. Then do a four-step dynamic programming count: set f_0(5,5)=1 and all other squares 0; for k=0,1,2,3 compute f_{k+1}(r,c) by summing f_k over all squares that can move by a knight to (r,c). After the fourth update, read f_4(3,3), which should give 54.

Use the text’s knight-move rule to list legal moves. Instead of propagating all four moves directly, split any four-move path into its position after two moves. Compute a table A(u) = number of two-move ways from the horse to each square u. Separately compute B(u) = number of two-move ways from the circle to each square u; this works because knight moves are reversible. Then sum A(u)B(u) over all board squares u. The midpoint dot product counts every four-move path from horse to circle exactly once and evaluates to 54.
